meta.title: AutoGen vs LlamaIndex: Which one to choose in 2026? (models, context & API pricing & code compared)
meta.description: Compare AutoGen and LlamaIndex architectural trade-offs, context windows, model APIs, and integration, and review side-by-side TypeScript to choose the right stack.

verdict: Choose AutoGen if your priority is orchestrating multiple LLM-powered agents that converse and collaborate to solve complex, dynamic tasks. Choose LlamaIndex if you need a robust framework for ingesting, indexing, and querying private data with retrieval-augmented generation. Many production systems combine both: LlamaIndex for data retrieval and AutoGen for agent coordination. Evaluate based on your primary need—agentic workflows or data connectivity—and consider integrating them for comprehensive solutions.

comparison.category: Core purpose and primary use case
comparison.toolA: AutoGen is designed for building multi-agent systems where LLM-powered agents converse with each other and with humans to solve tasks. It excels at orchestrating complex, interactive workflows such as code generation, debugging, and collaborative problem-solving. Its architecture centers on agent conversations and event-driven execution.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex is a data framework for connecting custom data sources to large language models. It focuses on ingestion, indexing, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), enabling applications like question answering over documents, chatbots with knowledge bases, and data-augmented agents. Its core strength is efficient data structuring and querying.

comparison.toolA: AutoGen uses a conversation-centric model where agents exchange messages to coordinate actions. It supports flexible conversation patterns, including group chats, hierarchical setups, and tool use, with an event-driven runtime for scalability. The framework emphasizes asynchronous messaging and human-in-the-loop interaction.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex employs a pipeline-based architecture for data processing: loaders, indices, retrievers, and query engines. It provides modular components for ingestion, transformation, and retrieval, with support for advanced indexing strategies like vector stores and knowledge graphs. Workflows are defined via declarative interfaces and can be composed into agentic systems.

comparison.toolA: AutoGen integrates with various LLM providers (e.g., OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, local models) and tools through a extensible agent interface. It supports code execution environments, web browsing, and custom tool integration. The ecosystem is growing, with community extensions and examples, though it is less focused on data connectors.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex offers a vast ecosystem of data connectors (e.g., APIs, databases, document formats) and integrations with vector stores, LLMs, and embedding models. It provides tools for evaluation, observability, and deployment, with a strong community and extensive documentation. Its integration breadth is particularly strong for enterprise data sources.

comparison.category: Ease of use and learning curve
comparison.toolA: AutoGen's API is relatively straightforward for defining agents and conversation patterns, but mastering multi-agent orchestration concepts (e.g., group chat management, termination conditions) requires understanding of distributed systems and LLM behavior. Documentation and examples are available, but the framework is evolving, so some features may change.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex provides high-level abstractions that simplify RAG implementation, with quickstart guides and templates. However, advanced customization (e.g., custom indices, hybrid retrieval) demands familiarity with information retrieval concepts. The learning curve is moderate, and the framework is well-documented with active community support.

comparison.toolA: AutoGen has a growing open-source community, primarily on GitHub and Discord, with active contributions from Microsoft Research and users. Support resources include documentation, examples, and research papers. The community is smaller than LlamaIndex's but focused on agentic patterns.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex boasts a large and active community with extensive documentation, tutorials, blogs, and a vibrant Discord server. It has strong enterprise adoption and commercial backing, offering paid support plans. The ecosystem includes numerous community-contributed integrations and extensions.

comparison.toolA: AutoGen's event-driven runtime supports asynchronous execution and can scale to many agents, but performance depends on LLM latency and orchestration overhead. It is suitable for complex workflows, though optimizing conversation patterns is necessary for high throughput. Benchmarks are workload-dependent and not universally published.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex is optimized for efficient data retrieval and indexing, with support for caching, async operations, and distributed vector stores. Scalability depends on the underlying vector database and configuration. It handles large datasets well, but RAG performance varies with retrieval strategy and data characteristics.

comparison.toolA: AutoGen provides mechanisms for sandboxed code execution and access control in agent interactions, but security depends on configuration and deployment environment. It supports human oversight and audit trails via conversation logs. Compliance features are not natively built-in; users must implement according to their requirements.
comparison.toolB: LlamaIndex offers data privacy through local processing and integration with secure vector stores. It provides access controls and encryption depending on the chosen components. Compliance (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA) is achievable via proper configuration and third-party services, but the framework itself does not certify compliance.

faq.q: Which tool is better suited for building a multi-agent system?
faq.a: AutoGen is specifically designed for multi-agent orchestration, with built-in support for agent conversations, group chats, and human-in-the-loop workflows. It excels when your application requires multiple LLM agents to collaborate dynamically. LlamaIndex can support agentic behavior but is more focused on data retrieval; combining both can leverage AutoGen for orchestration and LlamaIndex for data access.

faq.q: Can LlamaIndex be used for agent workflows without AutoGen?
faq.a: Yes, LlamaIndex includes agent capabilities, such as ReAct agents and tool use, allowing you to build agentic workflows without a separate orchestration framework. However, for complex multi-agent scenarios with intricate conversation patterns, a dedicated orchestrator like AutoGen may offer more flexibility. Evaluate based on the complexity of interactions your application requires.

faq.q: Which framework offers better data integration for RAG applications?
faq.a: LlamaIndex provides a comprehensive set of data connectors, indexing strategies, and retrieval mechanisms tailored for RAG, making it the stronger choice for data-intensive applications. AutoGen focuses on agent coordination and offers less built-in data handling. For RAG with multiple agents, you might use LlamaIndex for retrieval and AutoGen for agent orchestration.

faq.q: Are AutoGen and LlamaIndex compatible with each other?
faq.a: Yes, they can be integrated: LlamaIndex can serve as a tool within AutoGen agents to retrieve information from your data sources. This combination allows you to build agents that query private data via LlamaIndex while AutoGen manages multi-agent conversations. Integration requires custom code to wrap LlamaIndex query engines as AutoGen tools, but is feasible and documented in community examples.

faq.q: What are the licensing and cost considerations for each tool?
faq.a: Both AutoGen and LlamaIndex are open-source under permissive licenses (MIT for AutoGen, MIT for LlamaIndex), allowing free use and modification. Costs arise from underlying LLM API usage, vector databases, and infrastructure. LlamaIndex offers optional paid support plans, while AutoGen relies on community support. Always check the latest license terms for your version.

faq.q: Which tool has better documentation and community support?
faq.a: LlamaIndex has more extensive documentation, tutorials, and a larger community, partly due to its longer presence and commercial backing. AutoGen's documentation is solid but evolving, with a smaller community. For beginners, LlamaIndex may be easier to learn; for advanced multi-agent patterns, AutoGen's examples and research papers are valuable.

faq.q: How do security features compare between AutoGen and LlamaIndex?
faq.a: Both frameworks offer security features but require proper configuration. AutoGen includes sandboxed code execution and conversation logging for auditability. LlamaIndex provides data privacy through local processing and integration with secure vector stores. Neither is compliance-certified out of the box; you must implement controls based on your regulatory requirements. Evaluate security in the context of your deployment architecture.

faq.q: Can I use AutoGen and LlamaIndex together in a production system?
faq.a: Yes, many production systems combine both: LlamaIndex for data ingestion and retrieval, and AutoGen for orchestrating agent interactions. This pattern is common in applications like research assistants or customer support bots that require both knowledge retrieval and complex dialogue. Integration requires wrapping LlamaIndex components as tools for AutoGen agents, but it is a supported approach.
